nameStory: The "luminescent panellus" gets its magical name from its ability to glow in the dark! Here in New England, if you find these mushrooms on a dark night, the edges of their gills actually emit a greenish light - like nature's own tiny lanterns. The "bitter oyster" name comes from their intensely bitter, astringent taste that would pucker your mouth instantly.
description: The luminescent panellus is a small, fan-shaped mushroom that grows in overlapping clusters on dead hardwood logs and stumps. These little fungi start as tiny white bumps and develop into kidney or fan-shaped caps up to about 1.2 inches across. They're orange-yellow to brownish in color and attach to wood with short, stubby stems that connect off to one side rather than in the center. What makes them truly special is that New England specimens actually glow in the dark!

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Fan or kidney-shaped caps up to 1.2 inches wide, orange-yellow to brownish color, with a tough, leathery texture that feels dry to the touch

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Closely spaced gills that run down the stem, pale colored, and amazingly, they glow greenish in complete darkness - bring a flashlight to turn off and check!

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Short, stubby, tough stems attached off-center or to the side of the cap, often barely visible as the caps seem to emerge directly from wood

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: No distinctive odor, but if you dare taste a tiny bit and spit it out immediately, it's intensely bitter and astringent

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in dense, overlapping clusters or groups, never alone, creating shelf-like formations on dead wood

habitat: Look for luminescent panellus on dead logs, stumps, and trunks of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, especially on beech, oak, and birch. They're particularly common in mixed hardwood forests and can be found from sea level to mountain elevations. You'll often spot them on the same log for months, as they're very persistent once established.

seasonality.spring: New mushrooms begin appearing as tiny white knobs on dead wood, especially after spring rains. Early spring specimens are often the brightest glowing.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fresh caps developing continuously. The bioluminescence is often strongest during warm, humid summer nights.
seasonality.fall: Still actively fruiting and easily found, often in large clusters. Many specimens from earlier in the year persist and can still be glowing.
seasonality.winter: Old, tough specimens may persist through mild winters, though they become darker and less luminescent. Look for dried, leathery remnants.

funFact: These mushrooms are literally living flashlights - the same chemical reaction that makes fireflies glow also makes these fungi shine, and scientists have grown them in labs where they glow so brightly they can be photographed without any other light source!
confusionNotes: They're sometimes confused with other small bracket fungi, but the bitter taste, off-center stem attachment, and especially the bioluminescence (unique in New England) make them unmistakable. Remember: if it glows, it's definitely luminescent panellus!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bitter oyster," these have nothing to do with edible oyster mushrooms and should never be eaten. The "stipticus" in their scientific name means "astringent" - referring to that intense bitter, mouth-puckering taste that was once used medicinally.
compareHints: As the main Panellus species in New England, compare them to other small shelf fungi like oyster mushrooms, which are much larger, have central stems, don't glow, and aren't bitter. Unlike true oyster mushrooms that are soft and fleshy, luminescent panellus feels tough and leathery, almost woody to the touch.
